title: Buy the Book, Lose the Book: Netherlands’ Market Authority Challenges Bundled Educational Licences
content:
Blog post by Maarten Zeinstra

The Netherlands’ Market Authority (ACM) has warned educational publishers to stop bundling physical book sales with licenses to digital material, effectively making the educational books worthless after one year. The ACM identifies an expected market failure: an uncompetitive market where dominant publishers exploit buyers who do not sufficiently organise themselves. Individual secondary schools lack the power to negotiate fair terms, leaving publishers free to impose restrictive licensing conditions that eliminate the reuse of physical materials.

The case (ACM/25/199621) started in early 2026 with the announcement of a study into educational materials in the Netherlands’ secondary education sector. The ACM had previously received signals in 2024 that this market was not functioning properly, pointing to bundled sales that led to waste of educational material, vendor lock-in, and consumer inertia.

title: Ten Findings Policymakers Should Read Before Proposing Research Rights Reform
content:
In June 2026, the European Commission published an independent report designed to strengthen the evidence base for future decisions about implementing Secondary Publication Rights (SPRs) as well as a harmonised copyright exception for research. 

This was intended to complement the existing legal and survey-based analysis developed in the major 2024 report on how copyright and other digital laws could better support research. By exploring the potential costs and benefits for all parties, it would help prepare the way for the formal impact assessment process required before any new legislation can be proposed in Europe. 

It comes in the context of growing concern (also highlighted in the report) about whether Europe and its institutions can afford a scholarly communications model focused strongly on proprietary publishing, or whether alternatives exist.

With legislation potentially addressing these questions at most a few months away (at least on available information at the time of writing), the study merits another look.

title: €170 Million a Year in France Alone: The Price of Leaving a Secondary Publication Right Out of the ERA Act
content:
Maximising the impact of research is at the heart of the European Union’s plans to boost competitiveness and find solutions to both economic and societal challenges. In this, finding the most cost-effective way of enabling the sharing of insights and research outputs plays a central role, both within institutions and with the private partners and members of the public with whom they work. We also know that open access to research is particularly important for SMEs, as drivers of competitiveness.

There are serious and widely-held concerns about the sustainability of the way in which scholarly communication works today, with higher and higher costs and fewer and fewer freedoms to use the outputs from publicly funded research.

Despite this, the EU may be on the point of taking a step that risks fundamentally undermining these efforts, putting the current business model of a few large companies ahead of the clearly expressed wishes of the research and scientific sector as a whole.

Our message is simple: the forthcoming European Research Area (ERA) Act should include a Secondary Publication Right (SPR), which lets researchers share their work in an open repository.

title: Mapping the European Rights Retention Community of Practice: Mobilising Change
content:
Blog post by Clara Riera

Rights retention is gaining momentum across Europe. To make this progress more visible, we mapped where members of the European Rights Retention Community of Practice are based and where interest in it is growing.

Since KR21 project partner SPARC Europe launched this community in late 2024, it has grown to almost 725 members worldwide, with over 665 from 31 European countries. Its 11th meeting on 8 October 2026 marked almost two years of regular exchange among researchers, librarians, policy professionals and others working to advance rights retention. 

This new map is a simple way to visualise this growing community. It shows where members are joining from, highlighting the spread of interest across Europe and, more broadly, the community’s international reach. The map reflects one of the community’s main aims: supporting the development of rights retention in institutional policymaking as a route to achieving 100% open access in Europe.

title: Innovation Act, Industrial Access Charter, ERA Act: Who Will Fix Copyright for Research Partnerships?
content:
Right from the start of the current mandate of the European Commission, there has been an emphasis on promoting innovation. Seen as essential for ensuring competitiveness and resilience in an increasingly uncertain world, this has been a constant theme across legislation, policy and funding.

In this context, we have seen a drive to address Europe’s ‘Innovation Paradox’ – the fact that the bloc has a very strong research sector, but that this does not translate into new products, services, companies and markets. There have been important steps to address this by building stronger bridges between research and innovation, starting already in mid-2024 with the decision to combine the policy briefs on research and innovation under one Commissioner – Ekaterina Zaharieva.

2026 nonetheless looks set to be the year when things get a lot more concrete. Since last month, we have had a draft of a European Innovation Act. There has also been the new Charter on Industrial Access to Research and Technology Infrastructures. The planned European Research Area Act later this year, and copyright reforms next, both offer further opportunities.

title: Choose Europe… or Are Research & Science Better Supported by Copyright Laws Elsewhere?
content:
Europe fails researchers in 7 cases.

Europe faces increasingly intense competition for research talent. The Choose Europe for Science initiative responds by helping attract and retain researchers and by promoting Europe’s strengths.

To improve Europe’s attractiveness compared to its competitors, decision-makers will also need to assess how we compare to other jurisdictions on copyright and how well Europe’s regime works for researchers.

There is still plenty to do!

Choosing Europe for science means choosing Europe for knowledge, too.

Click a case to expand. (Open all · Close all)

Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan and the US all allow TDM on legally accessed materials in partnership with industry, bringing extra resources to research institutions.

In the EU and UK, commercial partners are excluded. Researchers must buy an additional licence for content they already legally access, if one exists at all, and publisher contracts increasingly even try to block non-commercial TDM, against EU law.

title: Poison Pills
content:
Copyright reform is again on the horizon in Europe. Not only is the 2019 Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market under evaluation, but the European Commission has also called for evidence about a series of potential reforms and, just yesterday, 29 September, launched a targeted consultation.

One idea on the table is a possible reform of the Union’s copyright exception for research, to facilitate researchers’ work when engaging with copyrighted materials. There will be plenty of discussion about the precise wording of this in the months and years to come.

In this context, we will see the contours of a broader question: what are the aspects of copyright law that need to be avoided if we want to uphold the interests of users, the institutions they rely on, and society more broadly?

These legislative ‘poison pills’ sharply reduce the scope and beneficial impact of otherwise potentially beneficial legislative provisions. When engaging in copyright reform discussions, it is therefore valuable to look out for these and highlight the threat they pose early on.

title: A Pact Against Gold-Plating the Research Exception?
content:
In the State of the EU address last week, Commission President von der Leyen announced, to some applause, the idea of a ‘Pact against gold-plating’.

This refers to when EU Member States implementing EU laws decide to add extra detail to the features of the official Regulation, Directive or other regulatory tool. While some of this is simple drafting to ensure EU laws fit seamlessly into national statute, sometimes it serves other goals, such as advantaging a given sector of that country’s economy.

The problem is that adding such provisions tends to make regulation more difficult to comply with. It also represents a barrier to cross-border collaboration by undermining harmonisation efforts.

Typically, efforts to address gold plating focus on things like product regulation or reporting requirements. However, the way in which national governments have implemented copyright exceptions – often under pressure from the entertainment sector – arguably provides another strong example.
